newsitem.title: USA: USW raising holiday cash for WHX strikers.
newsitem.headline: USW raising holiday cash for WHX strikers.

text.p: United Steelworkers union officials said the union will hold a special fundraising effort next month to raise Christmas money for its members on strike at WHX Corp a sign the union is digging its heels in for a long battle with the steelmaker.
"We don't need (WHX Chairman) Ron LeBow to have a Christmas," Mickey Forte, president of Local 1187, told Reuters. "We're going to stay out as long as we have to, to get what we want.
"Nobody wants (a long strike.) I'm very concerned about it."
Forte said the union will hold a flea market and auction next month and proceeds will go into a Christmas fund and distributed to striking steelworkers. About 4,500 workers are on strike at WHX.
Union members walked out on October 1 after their former contract expired and negotiations failed to produce a new one. The strike has idled eight steel plants in three states.
WHX is only operating its coke-producing plant using salaried workers. Coke is a raw material in steelmaking.

Company officials were not available for comment. Forte said the company's proposals during contract talks in Pittsburgh included work-rule changes and changes to the health-care plan the union was unwilling to accept, but the main divisive issue is pensions.

No contract talks are scheduled. Forte said the company has to propose restarting negotations. "We weren't the ones who left Pittsburgh," he said. "They have to invite us to the table...when we go back, it's not going to be crawling on our bellies, accepting whatever they want."

The union wants WHX to establish a defined benefit pension plan, which is funded regardless of hours worked. The company currently has a defined contribution plan, which is funded based on age and hours worked and is cheaper to fund.
WHX has steadfastly maintained it can't afford a defined benefit plan and offered an enhanced defined contribution plan to workers.
But the union wants WHX to use its $406 million of cash-in-hand to fund a defined benefit plan. "LeBow is sitting on that cash...he could use it to fund the plan," Forte said.
But the company also has maintained it needs the cash for debt and interest payments and capital expenditures.

Forte said most truck drivers are supporting the steelworkers in their strike and have agreed not to haul steel from company warehouses. But he said some shipments have been moving out because some drivers have ignored the union's plea to halt shipments.
